parent.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Queen's Knight Variation
parent.overview: The QGD with 3.Nc3 develops the knight and adds pressure on d5. The usual continuation is 3...Nf6, after which White chooses 4.Bg5 (pin; Black replies Orthodox 4...Be7, Cambridge Springs, Tartakower ...b6 or Lasker ...Ne4), 4.Nf3 or the Exchange 4.cxd5. Black holds d5 with ...e6, which gives a bulletproof centre but locks the c8 bishop; Black frees the game with ...c5 or ...e5, or ...b6 and ...Bb7. White's main plans are the minority attack (b4-b5 against c6) in Exchange structures, or central play with e4. Play is slow and technical rather than tactical, with a strong reputation for soundness, and the Cambridge Springs is the one trappy tactical sub-line.

parent.name: Ruy Lopez
parent.overview: The Ruy Lopez is the most extensively developed Open Game. 3.Bb5 attacks the knight that defends e5, building indirect pressure on the e5 pawn without the Italian's vulnerability to ...d5. This root (3.Bb5) is a crossroads: after the most common 3...a6 (about two-thirds of games) the Closed Spanish (4.Ba4 Nf6 5.O-O Be7 6.Re1 b5 7.Bb3 d6 8.c3 O-O 9.h3) leads to a slow, locked-centre manoeuvring game; the Berlin (3...Nf6 4.O-O Nxe4) gives a solid, drawish endgame-flavoured structure; the Marshall Attack is a sharp Black pawn sacrifice. White's central plan is c3 and d4 plus the Nbd2-f1-g3 knight route, while Black counterattacks on the queenside (...b5, ...Na5, ...c5) or breaks with ...d5. Theory is the deepest of any 1.e4 opening.

parent.name: Old Indian Defense
parent.overview: The Old Indian (1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6, here reached by 1.d4 d6 2.c4) is the pre-fianchetto cousin of the King's Indian. Black sets up ...d6, ...e5, ...Nbd7, ...Be7, ...O-O and ...c6, aiming at a Philidor-like central structure that is solid and defensible but a little cramped. The main line is the Ukrainian Variation 3.Nc3 e5 4.Nf3 Nbd7 5.e4 Be7 6.Be2 O-O 7.O-O c6 8.Re1, where theory considers White slightly better. It has never been as popular as the King's Indian; the bishop on e7 is less active than a fianchetto. King's Indian players use it to sidestep the Samisch and Averbakh. The data root also holds the Neo-Old Indian / Modern set-up (1.d4 d6 2.c4 g6), which transposes to King's Indian or Pirc-like structures.

parent.name: English Opening
parent.overview: White opens with the c-pawn to contest d5 from the wing, keeping the e4, d4, g3 and b3 options open until Black reveals a set-up. It is a flexible, hypermodern, mostly positional opening: not as sharp as 1.e4 or 1.d4, with the character decided by Black's reply and by transpositions into the Queen's Gambit, Réti or King's Indian. Principal branches are the Reversed Sicilian (1...e5, with an extra tempo for White), the Symmetrical (1...c5, often with a Maroczy bind) and the Anglo-Indian (1...Nf6 and 1...e6/...g6 transpositions). White typically plays Nc3, g3 and Bg2, and expands on the queenside with Rb1 and b4, or takes the classical centre with e4. The database root is a crossroads; its most-played continuations are transpositions to QGD (1.c4 e6 2.Nc3 d5 3.d4), the King's Indian and the Réti.

parent.name: Pirc Defense
parent.overview: Black plays 1...d6 and, after 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3, ...g6 and ...Bg7, letting White build the broad e4-d4 centre and then undermining it from the flanks with ...c5 or ...e5 (hypermodern: the bigger White's centre, the bigger the target). The root is a crossroads: 1...d6 can transpose to the Philidor (3...e5 or ...c6) or to the Modern. White's replies run from sharp (Austrian Attack 4.f4, 150 Attack 4.Be3 with Qd2, Bh6 and h4-h5, Byrne 4.Bg5, Bayonet h4) to unhurried (Classical 4.Nf3 with Be2 and castling, fianchetto). Typical play is imbalanced: White gets space and often a kingside attack, Black gets a solid fianchettoed king and counterplay on the queenside and with central breaks. It is sound but has a reputation for giving White chances; Kasparov doubted it for the top level (s1), though Caruana, Anand and Grischuk have used it (s2).

parent.name: Slav Defense
parent.overview: Black supports d5 with ...c6 so that the centre is held by pawns while the light-squared bishop stays free to come out (usually to f5 or g4) before ...e6. The root is a crossroads: after 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Nc3 Black chooses the Pure Slav with ...dxc4 (active bishop, ...e5/...c5 breaks), the Semi-Slav with ...e6 (c6-d5-e6 triangle, theory-heavy and often sharp: Meran, Botvinnik, Anti-Meran), or the Chebanenko ...a6. White can also play the Exchange (cxd5 cxd5), a symmetrical structure with queenside minority attack ideas that has a drawish reputation, or quiet systems with 3.e3 or 3.Bf4. The Slav is played by many world champions (Botvinnik, Smyslov, Anand, Kramnik) and is regarded as sound; sources treat it as solid with room for counterplay rather than a forced-draw defence.

parent.name: King's Gambit
parent.overview: 2.f4 offers a pawn at once to deflect Black's e-pawn, build a big centre with d4, develop quickly and use the half-open f-file against f7 (Bc4, Nf3, castling). The root covers both the Accepted lines (2...exf4: Kieseritzky 3.Nf3 g5 4.h4 g4 5.Ne5, Muzio, Bishop's Gambit 3.Bc4) and Declined lines (Falkbeer 2...d5, Classical 2...Bc5, and 2...d6 which is the most played move in the database). Accepted lines are sharp and tactically dense; Black tries to hold the pawn with ...g5 or return it with ...d5/...d6 to ease development. Declined lines are more solid and are chosen by stronger players who want to avoid the chaos. Play is open and double-edged for White's king as well.

alternative_names: Irregular Openings: Polish Opening, Birmingham Gambit

parent.name: Polish Opening
parent.overview: White plays 1.b4 to grab queenside space and fianchetto the bishop to b2, putting long-diagonal pressure on e5, f6 and g7. It is an irregular flank opening: Black chooses the set-up with 1...e5 (2.Bb2 Bxb4 3.Bxe5, the Exchange Variation, which equalises), 1...d5 (the German Defence 2...Qd6 etc.), or 1...Nf6 and 1...e6 reaching Indian-like or Queen's Gambit-like set-ups. The opening is sound and not refuted but gives Black no real problems, so it is rarely seen at elite level and chosen as a surprise weapon (Carlsen used it against Nakamura and So in 2021). Theory is small and the play is flank-oriented, with unbalanced pawn structures but typically no early forced tactics. Alekhine's complaint was that it reveals White's intentions before knowing Black's.

parent.name: Benoni Defense: Old Benoni
parent.overview: Black answers 1.d4 with 1...c5 before committing to ...d5 or ...Nf6; the root is a crossroads. White normally replies 2.d5, gaining space with a wedge, and Black then has to undermine d5 with ...e6, ...e5, ...d6, ...Nf6 or ...b5 so as not to be squeezed. Main branches are 2.d5 e6 (heading for a Modern Benoni structure), 2.d5 d6 3.e4 (the Schmid Benoni, with a King's-Indian-like set-up), and 2.d5 e5 (Czech Benoni, a locked centre with kingside play by f4 and queenside b4 for White). White can also play 2.dxc5, 2.e3 or 2.c3, which tend to transpose to other structures. Sources describe the opening as a long strategic space-versus-counterplay struggle, playable but demanding, rare at top level though used by Alekhine, Kasparov, Torre and Vaganian.

parent.name: Modern Defense
parent.overview: Black plays 1...g6 and 2...Bg7 and lets White build the e4-d4 centre, delaying ...Nf6 (which separates it from the Pirc), then attacks the centre with ...c5, ...e5 or ...Nc6 and the pressure of the g7 bishop. It is a simple, repeatable set-up that Black can adopt against almost anything, and its flexible move order makes it a practical surprise weapon. White's main tries are the Standard line (2.d4 Bg7 3.Nc3 d6 4.f4 or 3.Nf3), the Averbakh-style 2.c4 / 2.Nc3 set-ups, and c3 to blunt the g7 bishop; White often attacks on the kingside with f4, while Black seeks counterplay against an over-extended centre. Sources call it sound but with a risk of passivity or of letting White build an overwhelming centre; it is moderately popular (about 1.7% of games in 2025 on one database) with occasional master use (Suttles, Davies, McNab, Carlsen).

parent.name: Bird Opening: Dutch Variation
parent.overview: After 1.f4 d5 the game resembles a Dutch Defence with colours reversed and White a tempo up. White's main aims are control of e5 and the dark central squares with the f-pawn, usually 2.Nf3 followed either by a g3/Bg2 fianchetto or by e3, Be2, O-O and d3 or d4/c3 (Stonewall formation). Black meets it by fighting for the centre and the dark squares: a fianchetto with ...g6/...Bg7, or ...Nf6, ...e6 and ...c5, with ...Bg4 as a pin. The play is positional and both sides develop to optimal squares; the downside of f4 is a weakened kingside, so it is 'double-edged' for less experienced players. Sources say there is little theory, it can be a surprise weapon at club level, and the opening has been tried by strong players (Larsen, Carlsen, Nakamura, Karjakin) but is not popular at the top, with White scoring only about 46.7% overall.
